issues.item: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: The threat items 'Checking Behind' and 'Back to Wall' imply a persistent interpersonal pursuit/assault-style danger (someone following me, needing surveillance of the room) that is hard to reconcile with a life-threatening motor vehicle collision unless there is additional trauma content not represented elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: 'Institutional Failure' is not a natural fit with the rest of this MVC profile: the other items center on fragmented accident memory, mistrust of self/body, and hypervigilance, but this appraisal presupposes a salient protector/institution betrayal theme that is not supported by the trauma type or other selected items.

issues.item: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event' does not connect well to the represented triggers, memory, or appraisals. For an MVC case, avoidance is more coherently focused on travel, roads, vehicles, reminders of the crash, or internal trauma cues; avoidance of prior social contacts suggests a different maintaining process that is not otherwise represented.

vignette: John, a 68-year-old African widower and former dancer, has been grappling with the aftermath of a life-threatening motor vehicle collision he experienced several months ago. On that fateful day, John was driving home from a local dance performance when another car, swerving out of control due to road conditions, collided head-on into his vehicle. The impact was severe; the crash left him with significant physical injuries and profound psychological trauma. In the weeks following the accident, John's world began to shrink dramatically. He had come to believe that going out was dangerous, and even mundane activities like grocery shopping felt overwhelming. His fear of encountering situations reminiscent of the collision led him to avoid leaving his home as much as possible. This avoidance extended to social contacts; he no longer attended community events or gatherings with friends, feeling that being around people from before the event only served to remind him of how vulnerable and unsafe he was. John's therapist initially tried to engage him in processing the traumatic event, but John found it challenging to think about anything discussed in therapy. His mind would wander away from these topics, and he often felt an overwhelming urge to escape any conversations that brought up aspects of the accident. This avoidance extended beyond just thoughts; he also began to avoid places and activities that reminded him of his dance career, which had once been a source of joy and identity. The traumatic event left John with intense feelings of being unsafe unless his back was against a wall where he could see everything in the room. He no longer felt secure even within his own home; any unanticipated delay or loud sound would immediately trigger his fight-or-flight response, making him certain that something bad was happening. These heightened states of arousal made it difficult for John to relax and enjoy moments of peace. John also struggled with the memory of the event itself. He felt like he could only remember parts of what happened, leaving significant gaps in his recollection. Even when trying to recall specific details deliberately, accessing those memories proved challenging, making it nearly impossible for him to tell a coherent story about what occurred even to himself. This disjointedness left John feeling as though the full weight and horror of the event remained elusive, perpetually lurking just beyond his grasp. Adding to John's distress were the negative appraisals he had developed post-accident. He no longer trusted that he could do the right thing, believing his judgment was impaired. His body, once a source of strength and agility through dance, now felt unreliable-a constant reminder of how fragile life can be. Moreover, John harbored deep doubts about the institutions meant to protect him; he had come to believe that if anyone or any system were supposed to safeguard him, they had failed. Over time, these avoidance behaviors and negative beliefs began to take a toll on his daily functioning. His reluctance to engage in social activities led to feelings of isolation and loneliness, particularly since becoming widowed. Professionally, John's passion for dance was overshadowed by an overwhelming sense of vulnerability; he stopped attending rehearsals or performances, leading to the dissolution of relationships with fellow dancers. It took a severe bout of anxiety triggered during a routine doctor's visit, when unexpected noises in the waiting room set off intense panic, for John to realize that he needed help. He was most afraid of being trapped in his own fears and unable to reclaim any semblance of normalcy or joy. Seeking therapy became a desperate bid to regain control over his life, to trust again that his body could move gracefully without the specter of danger lurking behind every sound or delay. John's current state is one of profound vulnerability, but also hope-hope that through understanding and addressing these fears and avoidance behaviors, he might find a way back to the peace and security he once knew.
